title: The Respiratory System
description: Week 11, matched to the instructor's Exam 4 study guide: the upper and lower airways, the alveoli and the lobes, the breathing muscles and the nervous control of breathing, ventilation, respiration, perfusion, diffusion, and mucociliary clearance, arterial blood gases, risk factors and prevention, and respiratory distress, with a case study.

smoker.intro: A nurse on a medical unit is caring for a 71-year-old client who was admitted with shortness of breath that has been getting worse.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
Nurses' Notes

0800: Client reports getting more short of breath over 3 days and coughing up thick, yellow mucus. Smoked 1 pack a day for 45 years; quit 2 years ago. Worked 30 years in a coal mine. Drinks “maybe two cups of water a day.” Sitting on the edge of the bed, leaning forward with hands on knees; neck muscles tighten with each breath. Speaks in 3- to 4-word phrases. Restless, and keeps asking what day it is; daughter says this is new. Received a flu vaccine last month; has never had a pneumococcal vaccine.

questions.stem: A client with a head cold says, “My voice sounds muffled and flat, and my cheeks and forehead ache.” Which structures should the nurse suspect are swollen?
options: The paranasal sinuses, which help give the voice its resonance
The vocal folds of the larynx, which vibrate to make the sound of the voice
The turbinates, which make the air swirl so that it's warmed and filtered
The epiglottis, which closes over the larynx during swallowing
questions.rationale:
The paranasal sinuses (frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid) help give the voice its resonance and condition the air. Swollen, blocked sinuses make the voice sound muffled and flat, and aching cheeks and forehead point to the maxillary and frontal sinuses.

The vocal folds aren't the right answer: they make the voice, but swollen vocal folds make a voice hoarse, not muffled, and wouldn't explain the facial pain. The turbinates warm, moisten, and filter air, and the epiglottis protects the airway during swallowing.

Takeaway: Sinuses: resonance of the voice. Larynx (vocal folds): the sound itself, so hoarseness.

questions.stem: During an oral exam, a nurse sees swollen tonsils at the back of the mouth, just behind the arch at the back of the oral cavity. Which part of the pharynx is the nurse looking at?
options: The nasopharynx, behind the nasal cavity and above the palate
The hypopharynx, which leads into both the larynx and the esophagus
The oropharynx, between the palate and the hyoid bone
The larynx, where the vocal folds form the glottic opening
questions.rationale:
The oropharynx lies between the palate and the hyoid bone, and is separated from the mouth by the tonsillar arch, so tonsils seen at the back of the mouth are in the oropharynx.

The nasopharynx isn't the right answer: it holds lymphoid tissue too (the adenoids), but it sits above the palate, behind the nose, out of sight in an oral exam. The hypopharynx begins below the hyoid bone, and the larynx isn't part of the pharynx.

Takeaway: Nasopharynx (behind the nose, above the palate), oropharynx (behind the mouth, to the hyoid), hypopharynx (below the hyoid, into the larynx and esophagus).

questions.stem: A client recovering from a stroke coughs and sputters whenever drinking thin liquids. Which structure should the nurse suspect isn't sealing off the airway in time during swallowing?
options: The soft palate, which rises to close off the nasal cavity
The thyroid cartilage, the largest cartilage at the front of the neck
The cricoid cartilage, the ring at the bottom of the larynx
The epiglottis, which folds down over the opening of the larynx
questions.rationale:
During swallowing, the epiglottis folds down over the opening of the larynx (the glottis), so liquid goes into the esophagus instead of the airway. When it closes late, liquid slips into the larynx and triggers coughing.

The soft palate isn't the right answer: it also closes during swallowing, but it seals off the nasal cavity, not the airway to the lungs. The thyroid and cricoid cartilages form the framework of the larynx; they don't close over it.

Takeaway: Swallowing: the soft palate closes the nose, and the epiglottis covers the larynx.

questions.stem: A nurse is comparing the two lungs. For each feature, specify the lung it describes.
rows: Has three lobes
Has a cardiac notch, where the heart sits
Its main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical
Has only one fissure, the oblique fissure
Is covered by visceral pleura
questions.rationale:
The right lung has three lobes (upper, middle, lower), separated by the horizontal and oblique fissures, and its main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical. The left lung has two lobes, separated only by the oblique fissure, and a cardiac notch that makes room for the heart. Both lungs are covered by visceral pleura; the parietal pleura lines the chest wall.

The bronchus is the row most often missed: the right one is the more vertical, which is why aspiration goes right.

Takeaway: Right: 3 lobes, 2 fissures, the vertical bronchus. Left: 2 lobes, 1 fissure, the cardiac notch.

questions.stem: Nerve damage at the C3 to C5 level has paralyzed a client's diaphragm. Which finding should the nurse expect?
options: Breathing that stays normal at rest, since the intercostal muscles do most of the work
Rapid, shallow breathing, with the neck muscles tightening on each breath
Slow, deep breathing, since each breath takes longer to draw in
Labored breathing out, while breathing in stays easy
questions.rationale:
The diaphragm, supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5), is the main muscle of inspiration. Without it, breaths are shallow, the rate rises to make up for it, and the accessory muscles of the neck (the sternocleidomastoid and scalenes) work on every breath.

“The intercostals do most of the work” isn't the right answer: they do help, but they work mainly during exercise and distress; at rest the diaphragm does most of the work. Breathing in is what's impaired, not breathing out.

Takeaway: C3, C4, and C5 keep the diaphragm alive: the phrenic nerve. Without it, the accessory muscles take over.

questions.stem: During an assessment, a client sits leaning forward with both hands on the knees, and the muscles of the neck tighten with each breath. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
options: The client is working hard to breathe, and is using the accessory muscles
The client is in a position of comfort that doesn't point to a breathing problem
The neck muscles are tense from coughing, not from the work of breathing
The client is guarding against back pain, so the nurse should assess the spine
questions.rationale:
Leaning forward with the hands on the knees is the tripod position, which clients in respiratory distress take, and neck muscles that tighten with each breath are accessory muscles (the sternocleidomastoid and scalenes) helping to breathe. Together, they show a high work of breathing.

Tense from coughing isn't the right answer: coughing does use these muscles, but tightening with every breath, while leaning forward, is accessory muscle use. A position of comfort or back pain doesn't explain the neck muscles.

Takeaway: Tripod position plus accessory muscles = working hard to breathe.

questions.stem: Complete the following sentence about breathing in.
questions.text: During inspiration, the diaphragm {{0}} and moves {{1}}, which {{2}} the volume of the chest, so air flows into the lungs.

options: relaxes
contracts
downward
upward
decreases
increases

questions.rationale:
The diaphragm is the main muscle of inspiration and forms the floor of the chest. When it contracts, it flattens and moves downward, which increases the volume of the chest, and air flows in. When it relaxes, it rises again, and air flows out.

Picturing the diaphragm pushing up to breathe in is a mistake; it's the other way around.

Takeaway: Breathing in: the diaphragm contracts and moves down, and the chest gets bigger.

questions.stem: A newborn born at 28 weeks has alveoli that collapse at the end of each breath. Which cells are most likely not making enough of their secretion yet?
options: Type I pneumocytes, which line the alveoli for gas exchange
Type II pneumocytes, which secrete surfactant
Alveolar macrophages, which defend against pathogens and irritants
Ciliated cells of the trachea, which move mucus toward the throat
questions.rationale:
Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant, which lowers the surface tension inside the alveoli so they don't collapse at the end of each breath. In a very premature newborn, these cells don't make enough yet.

Type I pneumocytes aren't the right answer: they line the alveoli, but they're the thin cells where gas exchange happens; they don't make surfactant. Macrophages (dust cells) defend the alveoli, and ciliated cells clear mucus from the airways.

Takeaway: Type I: gas exchange. Type II: surfactant, which keeps the alveoli open.

questions.stem: A client's respiratory rate is 18/min, and the chest rises fully and evenly with each breath, but the oxygen saturation keeps falling as fluid builds up in the alveoli. Which process is most impaired?
options: Ventilation, the movement of air into and out of the alveoli
The nerves' control of the breathing muscles
Perfusion, the flow of blood through the pulmonary arteries
Gas exchange between the alveoli and the blood (respiration)
questions.rationale:
Ventilation is the movement of air in and out, and here it's working: a normal rate and full, even chest rise. Respiration, the exchange of gases by diffusion between the alveoli and the capillary blood, is what's failing: fluid in the alveoli thickens the barrier oxygen must cross.

Ventilation isn't the right answer: the client has a lung problem and a falling saturation, but air is still moving. Nothing points to the nerves or to blocked blood flow.

Takeaway: Ventilation moves air; respiration exchanges gases. A client can ventilate well and still not oxygenate.

questions.stem: A blood clot blocks blood flow to part of a client's lung (a pulmonary embolism), but air still moves in and out of those alveoli. Which describes the affected area?
options: Ventilated but not perfused, so no gas exchange happens there
Perfused but not ventilated, so blood passes through without picking up oxygen
Neither ventilated nor perfused, because the alveoli have collapsed
Ventilated and perfused normally, since the clot is in a blood vessel
questions.rationale:
Gas exchange needs both ventilation (air reaching the alveoli) and perfusion (blood reaching their capillaries). A clot blocks the blood, so the area is ventilated but not perfused: air comes and goes without any exchange, a ventilation-perfusion mismatch.

Perfused but not ventilated isn't the right answer: it's the other common mismatch, but that's the pattern of blocked or fluid-filled alveoli, as in pneumonia. Here the air moves; the blood doesn't.

Takeaway: Clot: air without blood. Pneumonia or a mucus plug: blood without air. Either way, oxygenation suffers.

questions.stem: A client with asthma uses an inhaler that acts like the sympathetic nervous system on the airways. Which effect should the nurse expect?
options: The airways narrow, and the glands make more mucus
The diaphragm contracts harder, so each breath is deeper
The airways widen, and the wheezing eases
The heart rate slows, so the client feels calmer
questions.rationale:
The lungs' nerves come from the pulmonary plexus. Sympathetic stimulation causes bronchodilation (and less gland secretion), so an inhaler that acts like it widens the airways and eases wheezing.

Narrowed airways and more mucus isn't the right answer: it's the textbook pairing, but it's the effect of the parasympathetic (vagus) nerves. The phrenic nerve, not the sympathetic system, drives the diaphragm, and sympathetic effects speed the heart rather than slow it.

Takeaway: Airways: sympathetic = bronchodilation; parasympathetic (vagus) = bronchoconstriction and more secretions.

questions.stem: A client who has asthma is prescribed propranolol, a beta blocker, for high blood pressure. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the first dose, and teach the client to keep the rescue inhaler close by
Check with the prescriber, since beta blockers can narrow the airways
Give it with food, since beta blockers irritate the stomach and set off coughing
Hold the client's asthma inhaler, and ask the prescriber whether it can still be used
questions.rationale:
Beta blockers (and NSAIDs) can cause bronchoconstriction, which in a client with asthma can set off an attack. The nurse checks with the prescriber before giving it.

Giving it with the rescue inhaler close by isn't the right answer: it sounds like a safe compromise, but it plans for an attack instead of preventing one. Food has nothing to do with the problem, and holding the client's asthma inhaler would make it worse; the question for the prescriber is about the beta blocker.

Takeaway: Drug history for breathing problems: beta blockers and NSAIDs (bronchoconstriction), ACE inhibitors (dry cough), estrogen (clots).

questions.stem: A client has smoked {cig} cigarettes a day for {years} years. How many pack-years is this?
questions.rationale:
A pack is 20 cigarettes, so {cig} cigarettes a day is {=cig / 20} pack(s) a day. Pack-years = packs a day × years smoked = {=cig / 20} × {years} = {answer}.

The usual mistake is multiplying the cigarettes by the years ({=cig * years}), which leaves out turning cigarettes into packs.

Takeaway: Pack-years = (cigarettes a day ÷ 20) × years.

questions.stem: A client who worked in a shipyard for 30 years has had worsening shortness of breath for a year. Given this occupational history, which condition should the nurse consider?
options: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis (black lung)
Byssinosis, from cotton and other fabric dust
Farmer's lung, an allergic reaction to moldy hay
Asbestosis, from asbestos fibers
questions.rationale:
Shipyard and construction work often meant exposure to asbestos, and asbestosis, a pneumoconiosis (dust disease of the lung), causes slowly worsening shortness of breath years later.

Black lung isn't the right answer: it's the best-known pneumoconiosis, but it comes from coal mining. Byssinosis comes from fabric factories, and farmer's lung (extrinsic alveolitis) from farm dusts.

Takeaway: Ask about occupation: coal mining (black lung), shipyards and construction (asbestosis), fabric work (byssinosis), farming (extrinsic alveolitis).

questions.stem: A client has sudden shortness of breath and chest pain. Which finding in the client's history should the nurse report as raising the risk of a pulmonary embolism?
options: Has hay fever each spring
Takes an estrogen-containing birth control pill
Had whooping cough as a child
Takes lisinopril for high blood pressure
questions.rationale:
Medicines that contain estrogen raise the risk of blood clots, and so of a pulmonary embolism, along with recent travel, immobility, surgery, cancer, and pregnancy.

Lisinopril isn't the right answer: it's a medication with respiratory side effects, but its side effect is a dry cough, not clots. Hay fever and childhood whooping cough belong in the respiratory history but don't point to an embolism.

Takeaway: Clot risks in a respiratory history: estrogen, travel, immobility, surgery, cancer, pregnancy.

questions.stem: A nurse auscultates the lungs of four clients. Which client's finding should the nurse report first?
options: Crackles at both lung bases in a client with heart failure, unchanged from yesterday
Scattered rhonchi that clear after a client coughs
A loud, high-pitched sound on each breath in, in a client whose lips are swelling
Expiratory wheezes in a client with asthma who used a rescue inhaler 5 minutes ago
questions.rationale:
A loud, high-pitched sound on breathing in is stridor, from a narrowing upper airway, and with swelling lips it points to an allergic reaction that can close the airway. Airway comes first.

The wheezes aren't the right answer: asthma can be serious, but the client just used a rescue inhaler, which takes a few minutes to work; that's a reassessment, not the first call. Unchanged crackles and rhonchi that clear with coughing are stable findings.

Takeaway: Stridor is an airway emergency. Airway, breathing, circulation decide who comes first.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client asks, “Why do I need a flu shot every year?” Which response should the nurse give?
options: “Flu viruses change, so each season's vaccine is updated, and vaccinated people tend to have milder illness.”
“Your immunity from last year's shot has worn off, and the same vaccine is given each year to renew it.”
“The vaccine treats the flu if you catch it, so you need it before each flu season.”
“Adults over 65 need it yearly, while younger adults need it once in 5 years.”
questions.rationale:
Many strains of influenza virus circulate, and they change, so each season's vaccine is updated to match. People who get the seasonal vaccine tend to have milder symptoms and fewer complications.

“The same vaccine renews your immunity” isn't the right answer: protection does wane, but the vaccine itself changes each year. It prevents illness rather than treating it, and yearly vaccination is advised for adults of every age.

Takeaway: Flu vaccine: every year, because the viruses change; vaccinated people have milder illness.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the upper respiratory tract. For each function, click to specify the structure that performs it.
rows: Holds the vocal cords, and is covered by the epiglottis during swallowing
Swirl the incoming air so more of it touches the moist lining
Traps particles in hairs and mucus as air first enters
Carries both air and food, behind the nose and mouth
Add resonance to the voice and make mucus that drains into the nose
questions.rationale:
The turbinates (nasal conchae) are curled shelves that make the air swirl, so it's filtered, warmed, and moistened. The paranasal sinuses are air spaces that make mucus and give the voice resonance. The pharynx is the shared path for air and food. The larynx holds the vocal cords and is sealed by the epiglottis during swallowing. The nasal cavity's hairs and mucus catch particles first.

Giving the sinuses the job of warming the air is a mistake. That's the nasal cavity and turbinates; the sinuses mostly make mucus and add resonance.

Takeaway: Nasal cavity and turbinates condition the air; sinuses add resonance; the pharynx is shared; the larynx makes the voice.

questions.stem: A client who works in a dusty warehouse asks what happens to the tiny dust particles that get past the mucus and reach the alveoli. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: Type 2 alveolar cells dissolve the particles in surfactant
Alveolar macrophages engulf the particles and clear them away
Cilia in the alveoli sweep the particles back up to the throat
Type 1 alveolar cells pass the particles into the bloodstream
questions.rationale:
Alveolar macrophages, sometimes called dust cells, roam the alveoli and engulf dust, microbes, and debris. They're the cleanup crew where the airways' cilia don't reach.

Cilia aren't the right answer: they clear the airways, but they line the trachea and bronchi, not the alveoli. Type 2 cells make surfactant, and type 1 cells form the gas-exchange wall.

Takeaway: Cilia clean the airways; alveolar macrophages clean the alveoli.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the cells of the alveoli. For each job, click to specify the cell that does it.
rows: Forms most of the thin wall where oxygen and carbon dioxide cross
Releases surfactant, which keeps the alveoli from collapsing
Engulfs bacteria that reach the alveoli
Divides to repair the lining after an injury
Is also called a dust cell
questions.rationale:
Type 1 cells are thin and flat and cover most of the alveolar surface: the wall gases cross. Type 2 cells make surfactant, which lowers surface tension so alveoli stay open, and they divide to repair the lining. Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) engulf germs and particles.

Giving repair to type 1 cells is a mistake, even though they're the main lining. Type 1 cells can't divide; type 2 cells divide and replace them.

Takeaway: Type 1: exchange. Type 2: surfactant and repair. Macrophages: cleanup.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the lobes and segments of the lungs. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The right lung has {{0}} lobes and about {{1}} segments, and the left lung has {{2}} lobes and 8 to 9 segments, which leaves room for the {{3}}.

options: liver
stomach
heart

questions.rationale:
The right lung has 3 lobes (superior, middle, and inferior) and 10 segments. The left lung has 2 lobes and 8 to 9 segments; it's smaller because the heart sits to the left, in the cardiac notch.

Giving the left lung three lobes is a mistake. The lingula is part of the left upper lobe, not a third lobe.

Takeaway: Right: 3 lobes, 10 segments. Left: 2 lobes, 8 to 9 segments.

questions.stem: A client has had a stroke in the medulla oblongata. Which finding should the nurse watch for most closely?
options: An irregular breathing pattern, with pauses in breathing
Loss of the sense of smell on both sides of the nose
A hoarse voice from swelling of the vocal cords
Wheezing from narrowed bronchioles in both lungs
questions.rationale:
The medulla oblongata holds the brainstem's breathing center, which sets the automatic rhythm of breathing. Damage there can make breathing irregular or stop it, so the nurse watches the breathing pattern closely.

Wheezing isn't the right answer: it's a breathing finding, but it comes from narrowed airways, not from damage to the breathing center.

Takeaway: The medulla sets the rhythm of breathing; damage there threatens breathing itself.

questions.stem: A client's airways are narrowing, and the PaCO₂ rises from 40 to 52 mm Hg. Which response from the brainstem should the nurse expect?
options: The medulla slows breathing so the narrowed airways can rest
The breathing stays the same, since the medulla responds to oxygen alone
The medulla signals faster, deeper breaths to blow off CO₂
The medulla stops signaling the diaphragm until the CO₂ falls
questions.rationale:
Sensors in the medulla respond mainly to rising carbon dioxide and the acid it forms. When the PaCO₂ rises, the medulla drives faster, deeper breathing to remove it.

Responding to oxygen alone isn't the right answer: low oxygen does stimulate breathing too, but in most people carbon dioxide is the main signal.

Takeaway: Rising CO₂ is the main trigger for faster, deeper breathing.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a client after chest surgery to hug a pillow against the incision while coughing. Which muscles mainly produce the forceful breath out in a cough?
options: The diaphragm muscle, which contracts and moves downward
The external intercostal muscles, which lift the ribs
The scalene muscles, which raise the first two ribs
The abdominal muscles, which push the diaphragm up
questions.rationale:
A forced breath out uses the abdominal muscles (with the internal intercostals). They squeeze the abdomen, which raises the pressure there and pushes the relaxed diaphragm up, so the pressure in the chest rises and air rushes out.

The diaphragm isn't the right answer: it's the main breathing muscle, but its contraction pulls air in; it relaxes to let air out.

Takeaway: The diaphragm and external intercostals breathe in; the abdominal muscles force air out.

questions.stem: A client who smokes asks why smokers get more chest infections. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Smoke thins your mucus, so it can no longer trap germs in the airways.”
“Smoke damages the cilia that sweep germ-filled mucus out of your airways.”
“Smoke kills the germs in your lungs, so your body stops building defenses.”
“Smoke narrows your blood vessels, so less blood reaches your alveoli.”
questions.rationale:
Mucociliary clearance is a key protective function: cilia beat to push mucus, with the germs and irritants trapped in it, up and out of the airways. Smoke paralyzes and destroys cilia, so mucus and germs stay in the lungs.

Narrowed blood vessels isn't the right answer: nicotine does narrow vessels, but the infections come from the damaged cleanup system. Smoke also makes more mucus, not thinner mucus.

Takeaway: Smoking breaks the mucociliary escalator, so germs stay in the airways.

questions.stem: A client's alveolar walls have become thick and scarred, but the client breathes at a normal rate and the heart pumps normally. Which process is mainly impaired, and which finding should the nurse expect?
options: Ventilation; the PaCO₂ rises because air can't move in
Perfusion; blood can't flow through the lung capillaries
Diffusion; the PaO₂ falls, especially with activity
Mucociliary clearance; mucus collects in the airways
questions.rationale:
Gases cross the alveolar and capillary walls by diffusion. A thick, scarred wall slows it, and oxygen is affected first, since carbon dioxide crosses much more easily. The PaO₂ falls, most of all with activity, when the blood moves past the alveoli faster.

Ventilation isn't the right answer: breathing feels harder, but this client moves air normally; the problem is getting the gas across the wall.

Takeaway: Thick alveolar walls impair diffusion, and oxygen suffers first.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing four clients. For each finding, click to specify which function of the respiratory system the nurse should expect to be impaired.
rows: Fluid thickens the walls between the alveoli and the capillaries
An opioid overdose has slowed the breathing to 6 breaths a minute
Years of smoking have destroyed the hair-like cells lining the airways
A weak heart pumps too little blood through the lungs
A broken rib makes deep breaths so painful that the client takes shallow ones
questions.rationale:
Ventilation is moving air in and out, so slow or shallow breathing impairs it. Perfusion is blood flow past the alveoli, which a weak heart reduces. Diffusion is gas crossing the alveolar and capillary walls, slowed by fluid or scarring. Mucociliary clearance depends on the cilia.

Calling the broken rib a perfusion problem because of the injury is a mistake. The pain limits how much air moves, so it's ventilation.

Takeaway: Ventilation moves air, perfusion moves blood, diffusion crosses the wall, and cilia clear the airways.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing four clients' arterial blood gases. Which client's results are all within the normal ranges?
options: pH 7.41, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L
pH 7.33, PaCO₂ 44 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 21 mEq/L
pH 7.44, PaCO₂ 33 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 23 mEq/L
pH 7.37, PaCO₂ 46 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 27 mEq/L
questions.rationale:
The normal ranges are pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaCO₂ 35 to 45 mm Hg, and HCO₃⁻ 22 to 26 mEq/L. Only pH 7.41, PaCO₂ 38, and HCO₃⁻ 24 are all inside them.

The last set isn't the right answer: its pH is normal, but its PaCO₂ (46) and HCO₃⁻ (27) are both just above normal. Check every value, not only the pH.

Takeaway: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45, HCO₃⁻ 22–26: check each value against its range.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a client's arterial blood gas results. For each result, click to specify whether it is below, within, or above the normal range.
rows: PaCO₂ 50 mm Hg
HCO₃⁻ 26 mEq/L
Base excess −1 mEq/L
PaO₂ 72 mm Hg
questions.rationale:
Normal ranges: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mEq/L, base excess −2 to +2 mEq/L, and PaO₂ 80–100 mm Hg. A pH of 7.33 is low, a PaCO₂ of 50 is high, and a PaO₂ of 72 is low; the HCO₃⁻ and base excess are normal. Together they fit a respiratory acidosis with a low oxygen level.

Calling an HCO₃⁻ of 26 high is a mistake. It's the top of the normal range, 22 to 26.

Takeaway: Learn the five ABG ranges; a value at the edge of a range is still normal.

questions.stem: A client's arterial blood gases are pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 58 mm Hg, and HCO₃⁻ 25 mEq/L. How should the nurse interpret these results?
options: Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis
questions.rationale:
The pH is low (acidosis). The PaCO₂ is high, moving opposite to the pH, so the cause is respiratory: the lungs are keeping carbon dioxide. The HCO₃⁻ is normal.

Metabolic acidosis isn't the right answer: the pH is low, but in a metabolic acidosis the HCO₃⁻ falls; here it's normal and the CO₂ is the abnormal value.

Takeaway: ROME: in respiratory problems, pH and CO₂ move in opposite directions.

questions.stem: A client's arterial blood gases are pH 7.49, PaCO₂ 30 mm Hg, and HCO₃⁻ 23 mEq/L. Which finding in the client's history most likely explains these results?
options: Three days of vomiting after eating spoiled food
Large amounts of watery diarrhea for two days
Breathing 30 times a minute during a panic attack
Thick secretions that partly block the airways
questions.rationale:
The pH is high (alkalosis) and the PaCO₂ is low, moving opposite to the pH: a respiratory alkalosis. Breathing fast during a panic attack blows off too much carbon dioxide.

Vomiting isn't the right answer: it also causes alkalosis, but that's a metabolic alkalosis, with a high HCO₃⁻. Here the HCO₃⁻ is normal and the CO₂ is low.

Takeaway: Low CO₂ with a high pH: think hyperventilation (anxiety, pain, fever, a ventilator set too fast).

questions.stem: A client has had severe watery diarrhea for 3 days. Which arterial blood gas results should the nurse expect?
options: pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 37 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 16 mEq/L
pH 7.50, PaCO₂ 44 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 32 mEq/L
pH 7.31, PaCO₂ 55 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 26 mEq/L
pH 7.48, PaCO₂ 31 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 23 mEq/L
questions.rationale:
Diarrhea carries bicarbonate out of the body, so the HCO₃⁻ falls and the pH falls with it: a metabolic acidosis (pH 7.29, HCO₃⁻ 16).

The high-pH, high-HCO₃⁻ set isn't the right answer, even though losing fluid from the gut sounds like vomiting. Vomiting loses acid (alkalosis); diarrhea loses base (acidosis).

Takeaway: Diarrhea: metabolic acidosis. Vomiting: metabolic alkalosis.

questions.stem: A client has had a nasogastric tube to suction for 4 days. Which imbalance should the nurse expect, and why?
options: Metabolic acidosis, from the loss of bicarbonate
Metabolic alkalosis, from the loss of stomach acid
Respiratory alkalosis, from breathing fast with pain
Respiratory acidosis, from shallow breathing with the tube
questions.rationale:
Suction removes stomach contents, which are rich in acid. Losing acid leaves extra bicarbonate behind, so the pH and HCO₃⁻ rise: a metabolic alkalosis, the same as prolonged vomiting.

Metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss isn't the right answer: that's what diarrhea causes; stomach fluid is acid.

Takeaway: Prolonged vomiting or NG suction causes metabolic alkalosis.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing clients' histories. For each condition, click to specify the acid–base imbalance it most likely causes.
rows: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Several days of vomiting
A piece of food partly blocking the airway
Anxious, rapid breathing
Kidney failure
A thiazide diuretic, with a low potassium level
A fever of 39.8 °C (103.6 °F) with fast breathing
questions.rationale:
Metabolic acidosis: diabetic ketoacidosis (ketones) and kidney failure (acid builds up and less bicarbonate is made). Metabolic alkalosis: vomiting (acid lost) and thiazide diuretics. Respiratory acidosis: an airway obstruction that traps CO₂. Respiratory alkalosis: anxious hyperventilation and fever, which blow off CO₂.

Calling fever a metabolic problem because the body is sick is a mistake. Fever speeds up breathing, which blows off CO₂: a respiratory alkalosis.

Takeaway: Match the cause to the system: lungs (CO₂) or metabolism and kidneys (HCO₃⁻).

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing clients at risk of metabolic acidosis. Which of the following conditions raise this risk?
options: Starvation
Prolonged vomiting
Severe hypoxia
Nasogastric suction
Watery diarrhea
A thiazide diuretic
questions.rationale:
Metabolic acidosis comes from extra acid or lost bicarbonate: starvation makes ketones, severe hypoxia makes lactic acid, and diarrhea carries bicarbonate out. Diabetic ketoacidosis, kidney failure, and dehydration are other causes.

Prolonged vomiting and nasogastric suction don't raise this risk: they're fluid losses too, but they remove stomach acid and cause alkalosis, as thiazide diuretics can.

Takeaway: Acidosis: starvation, DKA, hypoxia, kidney failure, dehydration, diarrhea. Alkalosis: vomiting, NG suction, thiazides.

questions.stem: A nursing student says, “In respiratory alkalosis, the blood has more hydrogen ions than normal.” Which response should the nurse give?
options: “That's right; the extra hydrogen ions are what raise the pH.”
“It has fewer hydrogen ions; that's why the pH is higher.”
“It has the same number; the bicarbonate level is what changes.”
“That's right; carbon dioxide adds hydrogen ions as it builds up.”
questions.rationale:
The pH reflects the hydrogen ions in the blood: more hydrogen ions mean a lower pH (acidosis), and fewer mean a higher pH (alkalosis). In respiratory alkalosis, carbon dioxide is blown off, less carbonic acid forms, and hydrogen ions fall.

“Carbon dioxide adds hydrogen ions as it builds up” isn't the right answer: it's true, but in respiratory alkalosis the CO₂ is low, not building up. (The instructor's list has this slip too; a higher pH always means fewer hydrogen ions.)

Takeaway: Acidosis = more hydrogen ions, lower pH. Alkalosis = fewer hydrogen ions, higher pH.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching how to read arterial blood gases. Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: In a respiratory imbalance, the pH and the PaCO₂ move in {{0}}. In a metabolic imbalance, the pH and the HCO₃⁻ move in {{1}}. A base excess of −7 mEq/L points to {{2}}.

options: opposite directions
the same direction
opposite directions
the same direction
a metabolic alkalosis
a respiratory acidosis
a metabolic acidosis

questions.rationale:
ROME: in Respiratory imbalances the pH and CO₂ move Opposite (pH down, CO₂ up); in Metabolic imbalances the pH and HCO₃⁻ move the same way, Equal. A base excess below −2 means too little base: a metabolic acidosis.

Reading a negative base excess as alkalosis is a mistake. Negative means a deficit of base, so the blood is more acidic.

Takeaway: ROME, and a base excess below −2 means metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis is breathing deeply at 32 breaths a minute. The arterial blood gases are pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 28 mm Hg, and HCO₃⁻ 14 mEq/L. Which explanation of the low PaCO₂ should the nurse give?
options: A respiratory alkalosis is the client's main problem right now
The ketones are breaking down the carbon dioxide in the blood
The lungs are blowing off CO₂ to offset the acid from the ketones
Anxiety is speeding up the breathing, with no link to the acid
questions.rationale:
The pH is low and the HCO₃⁻ is low: a metabolic acidosis from the ketones. The medulla senses the acid and drives deep, fast breathing to blow off CO₂, which pulls the pH back toward normal. The low PaCO₂ is the lungs helping, not the main problem.

Respiratory alkalosis isn't the right answer: the PaCO₂ is low, but the pH is acidic, so the main problem can't be an alkalosis.

Takeaway: In metabolic acidosis, deep, fast breathing lowers the CO₂ to help balance the pH.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the arterial blood gases of four clients. Which client needs follow-up first?
options: A client with pH 7.46 and PaCO₂ 34 mm Hg who is anxious about surgery
A client with pH 7.36 and HCO₃⁻ 21 mEq/L who is eating breakfast
A client with PaO₂ 82 mm Hg who is walking in the hallway
A client with pH 7.24 and PaCO₂ 64 mm Hg who is hard to wake
questions.rationale:
A pH of 7.24 with a PaCO₂ of 64 is a severe respiratory acidosis, and drowsiness shows carbon dioxide building up as breathing fails. That's a threat to breathing, so it comes first.

The anxious client isn't the right answer: the pH is slightly high, but a mild alkalosis in an alert client isn't as urgent. The other two results are normal or nearly normal.

Takeaway: Severe acidosis with a falling level of consciousness is a breathing emergency.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's risk factors for respiratory illness. For each finding, click to specify whether the risk factor can be changed.
rows: Is 79 years old
Smokes a pack of cigarettes a day
Sands and paints boats for a living
Drinks little water, and the mucus is thick
Belongs to an ethnic group with higher rates of asthma
questions.rationale:
Age and ethnicity can't be changed. Smoking, work exposures (dust and fumes, with protective gear), and hydration can. Dehydration thickens mucus and slows its clearance. (The instructor's list labels both groups “non-modifiable”; the second group is the modifiable one.)

Calling a job non-modifiable is a mistake. The client may not change jobs, but exposure can be reduced with ventilation and a fitted respirator.

Takeaway: Non-modifiable: age, ethnicity. Modifiable: smoking, hydration, work exposures.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old client asks which vaccines can help prevent pneumonia and other chest infections. Which response should the nurse give?
options: “A shingles vaccine, which also protects against pneumonia.”
“One flu vaccine at 65, which protects for the rest of your life.”
“A pneumococcal vaccine, which replaces the yearly flu vaccine.”
“A pneumococcal vaccine, plus a flu vaccine every year.”
questions.rationale:
The instructor's list for preventing respiratory infections: exercise, the pneumococcal vaccine, and the influenza vaccine. Flu viruses change each season, so the flu vaccine is needed every year; the pneumococcal vaccine protects against a common cause of pneumonia.

The shingles vaccine isn't the right answer: it's recommended for older adults too, but it protects against shingles, not pneumonia.

Takeaway: Older adults: pneumococcal vaccine, and a flu vaccine every year.

questions.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' notes that need follow-up.
questions.passage: Client reports [[getting more short of breath over 3 days]] and [[coughing up thick, yellow mucus]]. [[Smoked 1 pack a day for 45 years; quit 2 years ago]]. [[Worked 30 years in a coal mine]]. [[Drinks “maybe two cups of water a day”]]. Sitting on the edge of the bed, [[leaning forward with hands on knees; neck muscles tighten with each breath]]. [[Speaks in 3- to 4-word phrases]]. [[Restless, and keeps asking what day it is]]; daughter says this is new. [[Received a flu vaccine last month]]; [[has never had a pneumococcal vaccine]].
questions.rationale:
Worsening shortness of breath, thick yellow mucus, the tripod position with neck muscles working, short phrases, and new restlessness and confusion are signs of respiratory distress that's getting worse. Low fluid intake thickens mucus, and the missing pneumococcal vaccine is a gap in prevention to address.

The smoking and coal-mine history don't need follow-up: they're risk factors, but they're background that explains the illness, not findings to act on now. The recent flu vaccine is up to date.

Takeaway: In respiratory distress, act on the work of breathing, the mental status, and the gaps in prevention.

questions.stem: For each finding, click to specify what it most likely shows.
columns: A risk factor for lung disease
rows: Neck muscles tightening with each breath
A pH of 7.28 with a PaCO₂ of 62 mm Hg
45 years of smoking
Speaking in 3- to 4-word phrases
30 years of work in a coal mine
questions.rationale:
Using the neck (accessory) muscles and speaking in short phrases show respiratory distress. A low pH with a high PaCO₂ is a respiratory acidosis: carbon dioxide is being kept. Smoking and coal dust are risk factors that damaged the lungs over years.

Calling the blood gas a sign of distress is a mistake. It's a lab finding that shows the result of the failing breathing: carbon dioxide building up.

Takeaway: Sort findings into what you see (distress), what the labs show (acidosis), and why it happened (risk factors).

questions.stem: Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: The client's arterial blood gases show {{0}}. It's most likely caused by {{1}}, and the new confusion most likely comes from {{2}}.

options: a respiratory acidosis
a metabolic acidosis
a respiratory alkalosis
rapid breathing that blows off too much CO₂
the kidneys losing too much bicarbonate
narrowed, mucus-filled airways that trap CO₂
a reaction to the recent flu vaccine
high CO₂ and low oxygen in the blood
a small stroke in the medulla oblongata

questions.rationale:
A pH of 7.28 with a PaCO₂ of 62 and a normal HCO₃⁻ is a respiratory acidosis. The instructor's causes are an airway obstruction or lungs that can't exchange gas well; here, thick mucus and damaged airways trap CO₂. High CO₂ and a PaO₂ of 54 both affect the brain, causing restlessness and confusion.

Rapid breathing that blows off too much CO₂ isn't the right answer. The client is breathing 30 times a minute, but the PaCO₂ is high: the breaths aren't moving enough air to clear it.

Takeaway: Fast breathing doesn't always mean low CO₂: blocked airways can keep it high.

questions.stem: Which actions should the nurse take?
options: Raise the head of the bed to high Fowler's position
Give oxygen as prescribed and recheck the oxygen saturation
Report the blood gas results and the new confusion to the provider
Lay the client flat to rest the breathing muscles
Encourage fluids, unless they're restricted, to thin the mucus
Give the as-needed sleeping pill to calm the restlessness
Plan teaching about the pneumococcal vaccine
questions.rationale:
Sitting up lets the diaphragm move and the lungs expand. Oxygen as prescribed treats the low PaO₂, and the provider needs to know about the acidosis and the new confusion. Fluids thin the mucus so it can be cleared, and the missing pneumococcal vaccine is worth teaching about once the client is stable.

The sleeping pill isn't the right answer: the client is restless, but sedatives slow breathing, and the restlessness is a sign of low oxygen and high CO₂. Lying flat makes breathing harder.

Takeaway: Position upright, oxygenate, report, and never sedate restlessness from poor breathing.

questions.stem: Four hours later, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, click to specify whether it has improved, not changed, or gotten worse.
rows: Respiratory rate: 30/min then, 22/min now
Oxygen saturation: 86% then, 92% now
Speech: 3- to 4-word phrases then, full sentences now
Orientation: unsure of the day then, unsure of the day now
PaCO₂: 62 mm Hg then, 66 mm Hg now
questions.rationale:
A slower respiratory rate, a higher oxygen saturation, and full sentences show the work of breathing has improved. The confusion hasn't changed, and the PaCO₂ has risen, so carbon dioxide is still building up and needs to be reported.

Calling everything improved because the client looks more comfortable is a mistake. A rising PaCO₂ means the acidosis is getting worse, even as the oxygen improves.

Takeaway: Judge the blood gases, not just the comfort: a rising CO₂ is worse.

questions.stem: A few minutes after a bee sting, a client develops a loud, high-pitched sound on every breath in, heard without a stethoscope. Which interpretation should the nurse make?
options: Narrowed lower airways are making wheezes, which can wait for the provider's next visit
Fluid in the alveoli is making crackles, which repositioning will clear
Secretions in the large airways are making rhonchi, which coughing will clear
Swelling is narrowing the upper airway at the larynx, an emergency
questions.rationale:
A loud, high-pitched sound on breathing in is stridor, a sign of upper airway obstruction: here, swelling of the larynx from an allergic reaction. It's an emergency, since the airway can close.

The wheezes choice isn't the right answer: narrowed lower airways also make high-pitched sounds, but wheezes are usually heard on breathing out, and this sound comes with each breath in, from above the chest. Crackles and rhonchi are popping and low-pitched sounds from fluid and secretions.

Takeaway: Stridor on breathing in = upper airway obstruction: an emergency.

questions.stem: While laughing, an adult inhales a piece of peanut, which passes through the larynx and trachea. Where is it most likely to lodge, and why?
options: The right main bronchus, which is wider, shorter, and more vertical
The left main bronchus, which is longer and has more room
The right main bronchus, which is narrower and traps objects
The left main bronchus, which leaves the trachea at a straighter angle
questions.rationale:
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left, almost a straight line down from the trachea, so inhaled objects most often go right.

The left main bronchus choices aren't the right answer: the left bronchus is longer, but it leaves the trachea at a sharper angle, which makes objects pass it by. The right bronchus is the wider one, not the narrower.

Takeaway: Right main bronchus: wider, shorter, more vertical, so aspiration goes right more often.

questions.stem: A client who was sitting upright vomited and aspirated some of it. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The aspirated material most likely went down the {{0}} main bronchus to the {{1}} lobe, so the nurse should listen most closely over the {{2}}.

options: left
right
upper
middle
lower
lower back on the right
front of the chest under the right collarbone
front of the chest between the right 4th and 6th ribs

questions.rationale:
Aspirated material follows gravity and the straightest path: down the wider, more vertical right main bronchus to the lowest part of the right lung, the right lower lobe, which is heard best over the lower back on the right.

The middle lobe isn't the right answer: it's on the right too, but its bronchus branches toward the front, while the material falls straight down. The area under the right collarbone is the upper lobe, and the area between the 4th and 6th ribs at the front is the middle lobe.

Takeaway: Aspiration while upright: the right lower lobe, heard over the right lower back.

questions.stem: A nurse listens over a client's back only and hears clear breath sounds in every area, but a chest x-ray shows pneumonia in one lobe. Which lobe is most likely affected?
options: The right lower lobe
The left lower lobe
The right middle lobe
The left upper lobe
questions.rationale:
The right middle lobe, between the horizontal and oblique fissures, lies toward the front of the right chest, so it's heard from the front and the right side, not the back. That's how a back-only exam can miss it.

The right lower lobe isn't the right answer: it's on the right too, but most of it lies toward the back, so pneumonia there would change the sounds over the back. Both left lobes reach the back as well.

Takeaway: A complete lung exam covers the front and sides: the right middle lobe can't be heard from the back.

questions.stem: A client asks what the turbinates inside the nose do. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “They close off your airway each time you swallow food.”
“They hold lymph tissue that traps germs entering the nose.”
“They make your voice sound fuller as it passes through the nose.”
“They swirl the air so it's warmed, moistened, and filtered.”
questions.rationale:
The turbinates (conchae) are curled shelves in the nasal cavity that make the air swirl over the moist lining, so it's warmed, moistened, and filtered before it reaches the lungs.

The paranasal sinuses add resonance to the voice, the epiglottis closes the airway during swallowing, and the tonsils and adenoids hold the lymph tissue.

Takeaway: Turbinates: swirl, warm, moisten, filter.

questions.stem: A client with a stuffy nose breathes through the mouth all night and wakes with a dry, sore throat. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “The air skipped your nasal cavity, so it wasn't warmed and moistened.”
“Breathing through your mouth lets in more oxygen, which dries the throat.”
“Your sinuses drained into your throat and burned it overnight.”
“Your larynx stayed closed through the night to protect your airway.”
questions.rationale:
The nasal cavity warms and moistens the air. Breathing through the mouth skips that step, so cool, dry air reaches the throat.

Mouth breathing doesn't bring in more oxygen, sinus drainage doesn't burn the throat, and the larynx doesn't stay closed during breathing.

Takeaway: The nose conditions the air; the mouth doesn't.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks what the larynx does. Which answer should the nurse give?
options: “It warms the air and traps dust as you breathe in.”
“It carries air from the throat down into the two main bronchi.”
“It holds the vocal cords and guards the way into the trachea.”
“It drains mucus from the sinuses into the throat.”
questions.rationale:
The larynx (voice box) holds the vocal cords and, with the epiglottis, guards the entrance to the trachea, the last part of the upper tract.

Warming and filtering happen mainly in the nasal cavity. The trachea carries air to the bronchi, and the sinuses drain through the nasal cavity.

Takeaway: Larynx: voice and airway guard, the end of the upper tract.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching about the paranasal sinuses. Which of the following functions should the nurse include?
options: Making mucus that drains into the nose
Making the skull lighter
Exchanging oxygen with the blood
Adding resonance to the voice
Making surfactant for the airways
questions.rationale:
The paranasal sinuses are air spaces in the skull bones: they lighten the skull, give the voice resonance, and make mucus that drains into the nasal cavity.

Gas exchange happens only in the alveoli, and surfactant comes from the type 2 alveolar cells.

Takeaway: Sinuses: lighter skull, fuller voice, mucus.

questions.stem: A client who works in a woodshop asks how the nose protects the lungs from sawdust. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “The larynx coughs each particle back out before it goes deeper.”
“The alveoli push the sawdust back up into the nose to be blown out.”
“The sawdust dissolves in the warm air before it reaches the lungs.”
“Nose hairs and sticky mucus trap the particles as the air swirls.”
questions.rationale:
Nose hairs catch large particles, and the swirling air throws smaller ones onto the sticky mucus of the nasal lining.

Sawdust doesn't dissolve in air. Coughing helps, but it doesn't catch every particle, and the alveoli can't push particles back out.

Takeaway: The nose filters: hairs, mucus, and swirling air.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how swallowing protects the airway. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: During swallowing, the {{0}} folds over the opening of the {{1}}, keeping food out of the {{2}}.

options: uvula
epiglottis
soft palate
larynx
esophagus
nasal cavity
esophagus
stomach
trachea

questions.rationale:
The epiglottis folds over the larynx as the client swallows, so food goes into the esophagus instead of the trachea.

Choosing the uvula is a mistake: it rises to close off the nasal passage, but the epiglottis guards the airway.

Takeaway: Epiglottis over the larynx: food to the esophagus, air to the trachea.

questions.stem: A child's adenoids (the tonsil in the upper pharynx) are enlarged. Which finding should the nurse expect?
options: Hoarseness from swollen vocal cords
Pain with swallowing solid foods and liquids
Breathing through the mouth and snoring
A barking cough at night
questions.rationale:
The adenoids sit in the nasopharynx, behind the nose. Enlarged, they block air through the nose, so the child breathes through the mouth and snores.

Hoarseness and a barking cough point to the larynx. Pain with swallowing fits the palatine tonsils in the oropharynx more than the adenoids.

Takeaway: Adenoids block the back of the nose: mouth breathing and snoring.

questions.stem: A client breathes in hard during exercise. Which structure keeps the trachea from collapsing?
options: Smooth muscle that contracts with each breath
Surfactant that lines the inside of the trachea
C-shaped rings of cartilage in its wall
The pleura that pulls it open from outside
questions.rationale:
C-shaped rings of cartilage hold the trachea open, even when the pressure inside it drops during a hard breath in.

Smooth muscle changes the airway's size but doesn't hold it open. Surfactant lines the alveoli, not the trachea, and the pleura surrounds the lungs.

Takeaway: Cartilage rings keep the trachea and bronchi open; bronchioles have none.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the alveoli. Which feature makes them well suited to gas exchange?
options: Thick, muscular walls that squeeze the air into the blood
Cartilage rings that hold each alveolus open
Walls one cell thick, wrapped in capillaries
Cilia that sweep oxygen toward the capillaries
questions.rationale:
Alveolar walls are one cell thick (mostly type 1 cells) and wrapped in capillaries, so oxygen and carbon dioxide cross a very short distance.

Alveoli have no muscle or cartilage, and no cilia: gases move by diffusion, not by being swept or squeezed.

Takeaway: Thin walls + many capillaries = easy gas exchange.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the path of inhaled air. Which structures does the air pass through after the trachea?
options: The larynx
The pharynx
The alveoli
The bronchi
The bronchioles
questions.rationale:
After the trachea, air passes through the bronchi, then the bronchioles, to the alveoli.

The pharynx and larynx come before the trachea, in the upper tract.

Takeaway: Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

questions.stem: A client asks why the left lung has two lobes and the right lung has three. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “The left lung shares its space with the heart.”
“The left lung does less of the breathing work.”
“The left lung's third lobe is hidden behind the liver.”
“The right lung receives more blood from the aorta.”
questions.rationale:
The heart sits slightly to the left, so the left lung is smaller, with 2 lobes (8 to 9 segments) and a notch for the heart; the right has 3 lobes (10 segments).

Both lungs share the breathing work. There's no hidden third lobe on the left (the liver is on the right), and the lungs get their blood for gas exchange from the pulmonary arteries.

Takeaway: Left: 2 lobes, room for the heart. Right: 3 lobes.

questions.stem: A client's alveoli have been destroyed and merged into a few large air sacs (emphysema). Which change should the nurse expect?
options: More surface area, so oxygen moves into the blood faster
Less surface area, so less oxygen moves into the blood
Thicker mucus, so the cilia can't clear the airways
Stiffer airways, so air flows in more easily
questions.rationale:
Many small alveoli have far more surface area than a few large sacs. With less surface, less oxygen can diffuse into the blood.

Merging the alveoli lowers the surface area. Mucus is an airway problem, not an alveolar one, and the airways become floppier, not stiffer.

Takeaway: Gas exchange depends on surface area: lose alveoli, lose oxygen.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the mucociliary lining of the lower tract. Where should the nurse expect to find cilia and mucus?
options: In the pleural space around the lungs
In the alveolar macrophages
In the alveoli and the capillaries around them
In the trachea and the bronchi
questions.rationale:
Cilia and mucus line the conducting airways, like the trachea and bronchi, where they trap particles and sweep them up toward the throat.

The alveoli have no cilia; their macrophages clear what gets that far. The pleural space holds a thin fluid, and macrophages are cells, not a lining.

Takeaway: Cilia in the airways; macrophages in the alveoli.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the bronchi. Which statement should the nurse identify as accurate?
options: The trachea splits into two main bronchi, which keep branching
The bronchi are where oxygen crosses from the air into the blood
The bronchi connect the larynx to the trachea in the upper neck
The bronchi have no cartilage, so they can close off fully
questions.rationale:
The trachea splits into the right and left main bronchi, which branch into smaller bronchi, then bronchioles.

Gas exchange happens in the alveoli. The trachea connects to the larynx, and the bronchi have cartilage; the bronchioles don't.

Takeaway: Trachea → main bronchi → smaller bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

questions.stem: A client's chest x-ray shows that the lower lobe of the right lung has collapsed. How many lobes of the right lung are still working?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
questions.rationale:
The right lung has three lobes: upper, middle, and lower. With the lower lobe collapsed, two are still working.

One would be left only if two lobes had collapsed. Three is the full right lung, and four is more lobes than either lung has.

Takeaway: Right lung: 3 lobes. Left lung: 2.

questions.stem: When a client's diaphragm contracts during a breath in, what happens to the pressure in the abdomen?
options: It rises, as the diaphragm moves down onto the abdominal organs
It falls, as the diaphragm pulls the abdominal organs upward into the chest
It stays the same, since the diaphragm just moves the ribs
It falls, since the abdominal muscles fully relax
questions.rationale:
The diaphragm flattens and moves down as it contracts, pressing on the abdominal organs, so the intra-abdominal pressure rises (which also helps power a forceful breath out).

The diaphragm moves down, not up. It moves the floor of the chest, not just the ribs.

Takeaway: Diaphragm contracts: chest bigger, abdomen pressure up.

questions.stem: A client hyperventilates during a panic attack, and the PaCO₂ falls to 30 mm Hg. Once the client calms, which response from the medulla should the nurse expect?
options: Faster breathing, to keep the CO₂ low
Breathing that stops until the oxygen falls
Slower breathing, until the CO₂ builds back up
No change, since the medulla doesn't sense CO₂
questions.rationale:
The medulla oblongata responds mostly to carbon dioxide. With the CO₂ low, it slows the breathing until the CO₂ rises back to normal.

Faster breathing would lower the CO₂ even more. The medulla doesn't stop breathing to wait for the oxygen to fall, and it does sense CO₂ (through the blood's acid).

Takeaway: Low CO₂: slower breathing. High CO₂: faster breathing.

questions.stem: A client is struggling to breathe. Which muscles should the nurse expect to see lifting the upper ribs and the sternum?
options: The abdominal muscles
The internal intercostals
The scalenes and the sternocleidomastoids
The diaphragm and the external intercostals
questions.rationale:
When breathing is hard, the accessory muscles, the scalenes and sternocleidomastoids in the neck, lift the upper ribs and sternum.

The abdominal muscles and internal intercostals help push air out. The diaphragm and external intercostals do the work of every quiet breath in.

Takeaway: Neck muscles at work: a sign of hard breathing.

questions.stem: A client holds their breath for as long as possible. Which explains why the client is soon forced to breathe?
options: The blood runs out of oxygen within the first minute
The lungs collapse without a fresh breath of air coming in
Rising carbon dioxide makes the medulla override the hold
The diaphragm tires and starts contracting by itself
questions.rationale:
As the breath is held, carbon dioxide rises, and the medulla oblongata overrides the voluntary hold to start breathing again.

The oxygen doesn't run out in that short time, the lungs don't collapse, and the diaphragm doesn't fire on its own; it follows the medulla's signals.

Takeaway: CO₂ rising: the brainstem takes back control.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing quiet breathing. What do the external intercostal muscles do?
options: They lift the ribs up and out, enlarging the chest
They pull the ribs down to push air out
They raise the sternum just when breathing is hard
They close the larynx between breaths
questions.rationale:
The external intercostals lift the ribs up and out with each breath in, working with the diaphragm to enlarge the chest.

Pulling the ribs down is the internal intercostals' job, in a forced breath out. The neck's accessory muscles raise the sternum when breathing is hard, and the intercostals don't close the larynx.

Takeaway: Quiet breath in: diaphragm + external intercostals.

questions.stem: Which change in the blood most strongly drives breathing in a healthy person?
options: A rise in glucose
A fall in sodium
A fall in the oxygen level
A rise in carbon dioxide
questions.rationale:
In a healthy person, the strongest drive to breathe is a rise in carbon dioxide (which also raises the blood's acid), sensed by the brainstem.

A fall in oxygen also drives breathing, but it acts more weakly unless the oxygen is quite low. Glucose and sodium don't drive breathing.

Takeaway: CO₂ is the main signal to breathe.

questions.stem: Place the events of a quiet breath in, in order.
items: The medulla oblongata sends a signal to the diaphragm
The pressure inside the lungs falls below the air pressure outside
questions.rationale:
The medulla signals, the diaphragm contracts, the chest enlarges, the pressure in the lungs falls, and air flows in from higher to lower pressure.

Putting the air flowing in before the pressure falls is a mistake: air moves because the pressure in the lungs drops.

Takeaway: Signal → contract → bigger chest → lower pressure → air in.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the autonomic control of the airways. Which statement about the parasympathetic system is accurate?
options: It widens the airways during exercise
It has no effect on the airways
It speeds up the breathing rate when there's danger
It narrows the airways and adds mucus at rest
questions.rationale:
At rest, parasympathetic signals (through the vagus nerve) narrow the airways and increase mucus.

Widening the airways is the sympathetic effect, during exercise or danger. The autonomic system does affect the airways, and speeding up in danger is a sympathetic response.

Takeaway: Parasympathetic: narrower airways, more mucus. Sympathetic: wider.

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia becomes restless and confused, and the SpO₂ is 86%. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Encourage the client to lie flat and rest
Raise the head of the bed and give oxygen as prescribed
Document the findings, and then recheck the SpO₂ in an hour
Ask the client to cough and breathe deeply later
questions.rationale:
Restlessness and confusion with an SpO₂ of 86% mean the brain isn't getting enough oxygen. Raising the head of the bed eases breathing, and oxygen treats the low saturation; then the nurse reports the change.

Lying flat makes breathing harder. Waiting an hour or delaying coughing exercises leaves the low oxygen untreated.

Takeaway: New confusion with a low SpO₂: position and oxygenate first.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client in respiratory distress. Which finding should the nurse recognize as a late sign?
options: Restlessness
A fast heart rate over 100/min
A fast respiratory rate
Bluish lips and fingertips
questions.rationale:
Cyanosis (bluish lips and fingertips) appears late, once the oxygen in the blood is very low.

Restlessness, a fast heart rate, and fast breathing come early, as the body tries to make up for low oxygen.

Takeaway: Early: restless, fast. Late: blue, slow, drowsy.

questions.stem: A client who was calm an hour ago is now restless and anxious, with a respiratory rate of 28/min. Which should the nurse suspect?
options: Early hypoxia
Normal anxiety about the hospital stay
A need for more pain medication
Low blood glucose from a skipped meal
questions.rationale:
A new restlessness with fast breathing is an early sign of hypoxia (low oxygen): check the SpO₂ and breathing before anything else.

Calling it anxiety or a need for medication can miss the low oxygen. A low glucose causes shakiness and sweating, not fast breathing.

Takeaway: New restlessness: think oxygen first.

questions.stem: A nurse documents retractions in a client in respiratory distress. Which finding did the nurse see?
options: The skin between the ribs pulling in with each breath
The nostrils widening out with each breath the client takes in
The client leaning forward on the knees
Lips pressed together when breathing out
questions.rationale:
Retractions are the skin pulling in between or below the ribs as the client works hard to breathe in.

Widening nostrils is nasal flaring, leaning forward on the knees is the tripod position, and pressed lips is pursed-lip breathing: all signs of hard breathing, but not retractions.

Takeaway: Retractions: skin sucked in between the ribs.

questions.stem: A client can say only 2 or 3 words between breaths. Which interpretation should the nurse make?
options: A problem with the vocal cords
Anxiety about speaking to the nurse
Mild shortness of breath, which is expected after walking
Severe respiratory distress
questions.rationale:
Being able to say only a few words per breath shows severe respiratory distress: the client can't spare the air to talk.

Mild breathlessness still allows full sentences. The vocal cords would change the voice, not the number of words per breath, and anxiety doesn't explain it.

Takeaway: Short phrases between breaths: severe distress.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing an adult client. For each finding, click to specify whether the nurse should expect it or follow it up.
rows: Respiratory rate 16/min
Nasal flaring
SpO₂ 97% on room air
Sitting in the tripod position
Respiratory rate 30/min
Clear breath sounds in all areas
questions.rationale:
A rate of 12 to 20, an SpO₂ of 95% or more, and clear breath sounds are expected. Nasal flaring, the tripod position, and a rate of 30 are signs of distress.

Calling a rate of 30 expected is a mistake: it's well above the adult range of 12 to 20.

Takeaway: Flaring, tripod, fast breathing: follow up.

questions.stem: A client with long-term lung disease breathes out through pursed lips. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “It keeps your airways open longer, so more air can leave your lungs.”
“It warms the air before it leaves your lungs, protecting your throat.”
“It makes your diaphragm contract harder during each breath.”
“It lets you take in more oxygen through your mouth.”
questions.rationale:
Pursed-lip breathing creates a little back-pressure that keeps the small airways open longer, so trapped air can leave the lungs.

It doesn't warm the air going out, change how hard the diaphragm contracts, or bring in more oxygen through the mouth.

Takeaway: Pursed lips: slower, more complete breath out.

questions.stem: A mucus plug blocks a client's bronchus, but blood still flows past the alveoli beyond it. Which function is impaired in that area?
options: Perfusion
Ventilation
Diffusion
Mucociliary clearance
questions.rationale:
Ventilation is air moving in and out. The plug keeps air from reaching those alveoli, even though blood still flows past them.

Perfusion (blood flow) is intact here. Diffusion can't happen without air, but the first problem is ventilation, and the plug is a failure of mucus clearance, not its result.

Takeaway: No air in: ventilation. No blood past: perfusion. Thick walls: diffusion.

questions.stem: A nurse is explaining internal respiration. Which statement should the nurse include?
options: “Air moves into and out of your lungs with each breath you take.”
“Oxygen moves from the blood into your cells, and CO₂ moves out.”
“Blood flows through the capillaries wrapped around the alveoli.”
“Mucus is swept up toward the throat.”
questions.rationale:
Respiration is gas exchange. Internal respiration is at the tissues: oxygen moves into the cells, and carbon dioxide moves out into the blood.

Air moving in and out is ventilation, blood flow past the alveoli is perfusion, and sweeping mucus is mucociliary clearance.

Takeaway: External respiration: lungs. Internal respiration: tissues.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing diffusion in the lungs. Why does oxygen move from the alveoli into the blood?
options: The heart pumps the oxygen across the alveolar membrane
Oxygen moves from a higher pressure to a lower one
The cilia push it into the capillaries
Surfactant carries it into the blood
questions.rationale:
Diffusion moves a gas from higher to lower pressure. Oxygen's pressure is higher in the alveoli than in the blood arriving from the body, so it moves in.

The heart pumps the blood, not the gas across the membrane. Cilia aren't in the alveoli, and surfactant keeps the alveoli open.

Takeaway: Diffusion: high pressure to low, with no pumping.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the functions of the respiratory system. For each description, click to specify the function.
rows: Blood flows through the lung capillaries
Mucus is swept up toward the throat
Air moves into and out of the lungs
Oxygen moves from the blood into the body's cells
Oxygen crosses from the alveoli into the capillaries
questions.rationale:
Ventilation: air in and out. Diffusion: gases crossing the alveolar membrane. Perfusion: blood flow. Respiration: gas exchange, at the lungs and at the cells. Mucociliary clearance: mucus swept up.

Mixing up ventilation and respiration is a common mistake: ventilation moves the air, and respiration exchanges the gases.

Takeaway: Air, crossing, blood, exchange, and cleaning: five jobs.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the mucociliary clearance system. Which of the following can impair it?
options: Drinking plenty of fluids
Breathing very dry air
Smoking
Dehydration
Regular exercise
questions.rationale:
Smoking damages the cilia, and dehydration and very dry air thicken or dry the mucus, so the cilia can't sweep it.

Fluids keep the mucus thin, and exercise helps clear the airways; both support the system.

Takeaway: Cilia need thin mucus and no smoke.

questions.stem: After abdominal surgery, a client takes shallow breaths because deep breaths hurt. Which problem should the nurse watch for?
options: Too much air reaching the lower alveoli with each breath
Lower alveoli that don't fill and can collapse
A faster flow of blood through the lungs
Thinner mucus that drains too quickly
questions.rationale:
Shallow breaths don't ventilate the lower alveoli, which can collapse and collect secretions, raising the risk of pneumonia. Deep breathing and coughing help.

Shallow breathing brings less air, not more. It doesn't speed blood flow, and secretions tend to pool rather than drain.

Takeaway: Shallow breathing: poor ventilation of the lower alveoli.

questions.stem: A client with severe anemia has an SpO₂ of 98% but is short of breath on exertion. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: The SpO₂ reading is wrong, since anemia hides the true level of oxygen
The lungs can't move air in and out with anemia
Too little hemoglobin carries too little oxygen, even when it's full
The alveoli are filled with fluid from the anemia
questions.rationale:
SpO₂ shows how full the hemoglobin is, not how much hemoglobin there is. With little hemoglobin, the blood carries too little oxygen overall, even at 98%.

The reading can be accurate. Anemia doesn't stop ventilation or fill the alveoli with fluid.

Takeaway: SpO₂ measures how full, not how much.

questions.stem: At a high altitude, the air has a lower oxygen pressure. Which function is most directly affected?
options: Mucociliary clearance
Perfusion
Ventilation
Diffusion
questions.rationale:
Oxygen diffuses from higher to lower pressure. With less oxygen pressure in the alveoli, the difference is smaller, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood.

The airways still move air (ventilation), blood still flows past (perfusion), and the cilia still clear mucus; the gradient for diffusion is what shrinks.

Takeaway: Less oxygen pressure, less diffusion.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing four clients' histories. Which client has the most risk factors for respiratory illness?
options: A 24-year-old nonsmoker who drinks 2 L of water a day
A 40-year-old office worker who quit smoking 10 years ago
A 72-year-old who smokes and sands drywall without a mask
A 35-year-old runner who works outdoors in clean air
questions.rationale:
The 72-year-old has three risk factors: age, smoking, and an occupational exposure (dust from sanding).

The others have few or none: good hydration, quitting smoking long ago, and clean outdoor work lower the risk.

Takeaway: Respiratory risk: age, ethnicity, hydration, smoking, work exposures.

questions.stem: A client asks how regular exercise helps prevent respiratory infections. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “It strengthens your breathing muscles and your immune system.”
“It makes your lungs grow new alveoli each week.”
“It replaces the need for the yearly flu and pneumonia vaccines.”
“It keeps you from breathing in any germs while you move.”
questions.rationale:
Regular exercise strengthens the breathing muscles, helps clear the airways, and supports the immune system, one of the instructor's ways to prevent respiratory infections.

Exercise doesn't grow new alveoli or replace vaccines, and it doesn't stop germs from being inhaled.

Takeaway: Prevention: exercise, flu vaccine, pneumococcal vaccine.

questions.stem: A client who doesn't smoke lives with a heavy smoker. Which statement should the nurse include?
options: “Secondhand smoke doesn't affect the people who don't smoke it.”
“Secondhand smoke raises your risk of respiratory illness too.”
“The smoker's lungs absorb the harmful chemicals, not yours.”
“Opening a window clears the risk from the smoke.”
questions.rationale:
Secondhand smoke carries the same irritants and toxins, so it raises the risk of respiratory illness for others in the home.

Saying it doesn't affect nonsmokers, or that just the smoker absorbs it, isn't true, and an open window doesn't clear the smoke.

Takeaway: Smoke harms everyone who breathes it.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing three clients. For each client, click to specify the modifiable risk factor the nurse should focus on.
rows: A miner who doesn't wear a mask underground
A client who drinks one glass of water a day
A 34-year-old who smokes a pack a day
A painter who sprays in a closed garage
questions.rationale:
The miner and the painter breathe in dust and fumes at work, the client with one glass of water a day is poorly hydrated, and the 34-year-old smokes.

Focusing on age or ethnicity would be a mistake here: they can't be changed, so teaching aims at the modifiable risks.

Takeaway: Teach to what can change: smoking, work exposures, hydration.

questions.stem: A client who smokes asks which single change would lower the risk of respiratory illness the most. Which answer should the nurse give?
options: “Drinking more water each day.”
“Taking a daily multivitamin.”
“Quitting smoking.”
“Moving to a warmer climate.”
questions.rationale:
Quitting smoking lets the cilia recover and removes the biggest modifiable risk for lung disease and infection.

Hydration helps, but much less than quitting. Vitamins and climate don't address the main risk.

Takeaway: For a smoker, quitting matters most.

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old asks whether the flu vaccine is needed. Which response should the nurse give?
options: “It's needed just by adults over 65 and young children.”
“One dose protects you for about 10 years at a time.”
“It's needed if you've had the flu before, to prevent another case.”
“It's recommended every year for nearly everyone over 6 months.”
questions.rationale:
The influenza vaccine is recommended every year for nearly everyone 6 months and older, since the viruses change.

It isn't limited to older adults or to people who've had the flu, and one dose doesn't last for years.

Takeaway: Flu vaccine: every year, for nearly everyone.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client asks why the pneumococcal vaccine is recommended at this age. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Pneumococcal pneumonia is more common and serious as you age.”
“The pneumococcal vaccine replaces your yearly flu shot after 65.”
“It treats any lung infection you already have.”
“It's needed because your lungs stop making mucus with age.”
questions.rationale:
Pneumococcal infections, like pneumonia, become more common and more serious with age, so the vaccine is recommended for older adults.

It doesn't replace the flu vaccine, it prevents rather than treats infection, and the lungs don't stop making mucus with age.

Takeaway: Older adults: pneumococcal vaccine plus the yearly flu vaccine.

questions.stem: A client's arterial blood gases are pH 7.31, PaCO₂ 52 mm Hg, and HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L. Which finding in the history most likely explains them?
options: Several days of vomiting
A panic attack with fast breathing
Diabetic ketoacidosis
An airway blocked by thick mucus
questions.rationale:
A low pH with a high PaCO₂ and a normal HCO₃⁻ is respiratory acidosis: CO₂ is building up, as when an airway is blocked.

Vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis, fast breathing respiratory alkalosis, and ketoacidosis metabolic acidosis, with a low HCO₃⁻.

Takeaway: High CO₂ and low pH: the lungs aren't getting rid of CO₂.

questions.stem: A client's base excess is +6 mEq/L (expected −2 to +2). Which interpretation should the nurse make?
options: There's too much base, a pattern of metabolic alkalosis
There's too little base, a pattern of metabolic acidosis
There's too much CO₂, a pattern of respiratory acidosis
The result is within the expected range
questions.rationale:
The base excess shows the metabolic side: above +2 means extra base (bicarbonate), a metabolic alkalosis pattern.

A negative base excess (below −2) means too little base, metabolic acidosis. CO₂ is the respiratory side, read from the PaCO₂, and +6 is outside the expected range.

Takeaway: Base excess: positive = too much base; negative = too little.

questions.stem: A client's PaO₂ is 68 mm Hg. Which interpretation should the nurse make?
options: It's within the expected range of 60 to 80 mm Hg for adults
It's high, which suggests the client is getting too much oxygen
It's below the expected 80 to 100, so the blood oxygen is low
It shows a metabolic acidosis
questions.rationale:
The expected PaO₂ is 80 to 100 mm Hg, so 68 is low (hypoxemia).

60 to 80 isn't the expected range, and 68 isn't high. The PaO₂ measures oxygen; acid-base problems are read from the pH, PaCO₂, and HCO₃⁻.

Takeaway: PaO₂: 80 to 100.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing four clients' arterial blood gases. For each set of results, click to specify the imbalance the nurse should identify.
rows: pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 40, HCO₃⁻ 16
pH 7.50, PaCO₂ 41, HCO₃⁻ 33
pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 55, HCO₃⁻ 25
pH 7.52, PaCO₂ 29, HCO₃⁻ 24
questions.rationale:
Read the pH, then find the value that explains it: a low pH with a low HCO₃⁻ is metabolic acidosis; a high pH with a high HCO₃⁻ is metabolic alkalosis; a low pH with a high PaCO₂ is respiratory acidosis; and a high pH with a low PaCO₂ is respiratory alkalosis.

Naming the imbalance from the PaCO₂ alone is a mistake: in the first two, the PaCO₂ is normal, and the HCO₃⁻ explains the pH.

Takeaway: pH first; then whichever of PaCO₂ or HCO₃⁻ matches it.

questions.stem: A client has eaten almost nothing for several days. Which arterial blood gas pattern should the nurse expect?
options: A high pH with a high HCO₃⁻
A high pH with a low PaCO₂
A low pH with a high PaCO₂
A low pH with a low HCO₃⁻
questions.rationale:
Starvation makes the body burn fat, producing ketoacids: a metabolic acidosis, with a low pH and a low HCO₃⁻.

A high pH with a high HCO₃⁻ is metabolic alkalosis, and a high pH with a low PaCO₂ is respiratory alkalosis. A high PaCO₂ points to the lungs.

Takeaway: Starvation, like DKA: ketones → metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: A client with a fever of 103°F (39.4°C) is breathing fast. Which change in the arterial blood gases should the nurse expect?
options: The PaCO₂ falls and the pH rises
The PaCO₂ rises and the pH falls
The HCO₃⁻ falls and the pH falls
The HCO₃⁻ rises and the pH rises
questions.rationale:
A fever speeds the breathing, which blows off CO₂: the PaCO₂ falls and the pH rises, a respiratory alkalosis.

A rising PaCO₂ comes with slow or blocked breathing. Changes led by the HCO₃⁻ are metabolic, not the result of fast breathing.

Takeaway: Fast breathing: CO₂ down, pH up.

questions.stem: A client with kidney failure has missed two dialysis treatments. Which imbalance should the nurse expect?
options: Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
questions.rationale:
Failing kidneys can't get rid of acid or make enough bicarbonate, so acid builds up: a metabolic acidosis.

The lungs aren't the cause here, so it isn't respiratory. Metabolic alkalosis comes from losing acid, as with vomiting or suction.

Takeaway: Kidney failure: acid stays in, metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing metabolic acidosis. Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: In metabolic acidosis, the {{0}} falls, and the pH {{1}}. The lungs try to make up for it by breathing {{2}} to blow off CO₂.

options: PaCO₂
HCO₃⁻
PaO₂
rises
stays the same
falls
slower and shallower
faster and deeper
in short gasps with pauses

questions.rationale:
Metabolic acidosis lowers the HCO₃⁻ and the pH. The lungs respond by breathing faster and deeper, blowing off CO₂ to raise the pH.

Choosing the PaCO₂ as the value that falls first is a mistake: it falls only as the lungs make up for the acid.

Takeaway: Metabolic acidosis: HCO₃⁻ down, pH down, breathing up.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing clients at risk of respiratory acidosis. Which of the following conditions raise this risk?
options: Severe diarrhea from a bowel infection
Fast breathing during a panic attack
Several days of vomiting after a stomach virus
A mucus plug blocking a large airway
Severe pneumonia, with fluid in the alveoli
questions.rationale:
Respiratory acidosis comes from CO₂ that can't leave: an obstructed airway, or lungs that can't diffuse it, like fluid-filled alveoli in severe pneumonia.

Fast breathing lowers the CO₂ (respiratory alkalosis). Vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis, and diarrhea metabolic acidosis.

Takeaway: Respiratory acidosis: blocked airways or lungs that can't get CO₂ out.

questions.stem: A client is severely dehydrated after days of poor intake in hot weather. Which imbalance should the nurse expect?
options: Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis
questions.rationale:
Severe dehydration reduces blood flow to the tissues and kidneys, so acid builds up: a metabolic acidosis, one of the causes on the instructor's list.

The lungs aren't the cause, so it isn't respiratory, and dehydration from poor intake doesn't cause the acid loss of metabolic alkalosis.

Takeaway: Dehydration, starvation, kidney failure, DKA, diarrhea: metabolic acidosis.
